statuses.Demonstrated: The current material shows the whole observable. Either a theorem or derivation chain (Lean or paper proof) whose premises need no confirmation from the executable model: established mathematics, the OPH axioms A1-A3 and the declared basis, and premises the model demonstrates. Or a committed executable result of the model (main candidate Interval Echo) whose observer records exhibit the observable. For a premise: the executable model satisfies it, or it is established mathematics.
statuses.Conditional: Proved (Lean or paper), but at least one premise needs confirmation from the executable model that the current material does not supply: a physical attachment or identification, a regime, continuum or refinement assumption, or a realization of a structure on the native process. The row names those premises.
statuses.Partial: The material shows part of the observable: some of its clauses, a restricted domain or preparation, a candidate other than the main one, a computation without a theorem for the full claim, or a retrospective comparison. The summary states the covered part and the missing part.
statuses.Open: No result in the current material. The work is in progress.

rows.name: The Born rule
rows.what: Measurement outcomes occur with probabilities given by the squared amplitude of the quantum state.
rows.why: OPH has to recover quantum probabilities from observer records alone; the rule underlies every quantum prediction.

rows.name: State update (Lueders rule)
rows.what: After a sharp measurement the quantum state is projected onto the observed outcome, so repeating the measurement returns the same result.
rows.why: Repeatable records require this update; OPH must single it out among instruments with identical probabilities, since every later prediction starts from the updated state.

rows.name: Tsirelson bound 2 sqrt 2
rows.what: Quantum correlations between two separated measurements reach a CHSH value of at most 2 sqrt 2, above the classical limit of 2.
rows.why: Reproducing exactly this ceiling shows that OPH's local record algebras are quantum: stronger than classical records, weaker than arbitrary no-signalling correlations.

rows.name: Bell nonlocality in public records
rows.what: Measurements on separated entangled systems, with independently chosen settings, show correlations that no local hidden-variable model can produce.
rows.why: OPH builds the world from public observer records; it has to produce these violations from its own dynamics while each local record stays classical.

rows.name: No-cloning theorem
rows.what: No physical process can copy an arbitrary unknown quantum state; only mutually orthogonal states can be duplicated faithfully.
rows.why: OPH treats public records as copyable classical facts; the theorem draws the line between such records and private quantum information.

rows.name: Robertson uncertainty relation
rows.what: For any quantum state, the product of the spreads of two observables is bounded below by half the magnitude of their commutator's expectation value.
rows.why: Incompatible questions cannot both have sharp answers for any observer; in OPH this trade-off follows from the finite algebra of record events.

rows.name: Superselection and partition pinching
rows.what: Some quantities, such as total charge, divide quantum states into sectors whose superpositions no physical measurement can distinguish from classical mixtures.
rows.why: In OPH, sectors that observers cannot address coherently become the public, classical part of the record algebra; this links superselection to classical facts.

rows.name: Complex Hilbert space
rows.what: Quantum states live in a complex Hilbert space; amplitudes carry phases, and real-amplitude quantum theory makes different predictions in certain network experiments.
rows.why: OPH has to explain where the phase that observers track comes from; interference, unitary evolution and the Born rule all rest on complex amplitudes.

rows.name: Schroedinger evolution
rows.what: Between measurements, an isolated quantum system evolves continuously and reversibly by a unitary operator generated by its Hamiltonian.
rows.why: Any continuous symmetry flow of OPH's finite record algebra has a Hamiltonian generator, so reversible quantum dynamics follows from the structure of records.

rows.name: Measurement inside an interacting process
rows.what: A measurement is a physical interaction in which an apparatus writes a lasting record of a system's state.
rows.why: OPH starts from observer records, so its own dynamics has to produce the record-writing step without an outside measurement postulate.

rows.name: Decoherence and classical records
rows.what: Interaction with an environment suppresses interference between alternatives; once a which-path record exists, superpositions behave like classical mixtures.
rows.why: In OPH classical facts are records many observers hold; the theory has to show how such records form and erase interference.

rows.name: No-signalling and locality
rows.what: Local operations on one system cannot change the measurement statistics of a distant system; correlations alone carry no usable signal.
rows.why: Overlapping OPH observers must agree on shared records; no observer can steer another's statistics unless a record carries the influence.

rows.name: Pauli matrices and spin-1/2 minimal coupling
rows.what: A spin-1/2 particle in a magnetic field couples through the Pauli matrices, giving a magnetic moment with gyromagnetic factor g = 2.
rows.why: The Pauli square ties the spin term to the field strength; every charged spin-1/2 particle OPH describes depends on this coupling.

rows.name: Spin-statistics connection
rows.what: Particles with half-integer spin are fermions obeying exclusion, and particles with integer spin are bosons; the exchange sign follows the spin.
rows.why: Atoms, chemistry and stable matter rest on Pauli exclusion; OPH has to obtain fermionic exchange signs for its half-integer-spin excitations.

rows.name: Three spatial dimensions
rows.what: Observers locate events using three independent spatial directions, and measured distances obey three-dimensional Euclidean geometry at everyday scales.
rows.why: OPH reads the three directions from the slow response band of its icosahedral observer cell; every spatial prediction depends on that reading.

rows.name: 1+3 Lorentzian signature
rows.what: Spacetime has one time direction and three space directions, with a metric of signature (1,3) that separates timelike from spacelike intervals.
rows.why: In OPH one record-ordering direction plus three response directions give this signature, the causal structure every observer uses.

rows.name: Lorentz group SO+(3,1)
rows.what: Physical laws take the same form for all inertial observers, related by boosts and rotations forming the proper orthochronous Lorentz group SO+(3,1).
rows.why: Changing observer acts on each observer's celestial sphere by a conformal map; in OPH the Lorentz group is the group of these maps.

rows.name: Finite signal speed (light cone)
rows.what: No signal travels faster than light, and all observers measure the same maximal speed, which defines the light cone of each event.
rows.why: OPH attributes the limit to repair records crossing at most one seam per step; causality and relativity in the theory rest on it.

rows.name: Causal order
rows.what: Events are partially ordered by cause and effect, and every observer agrees which events can influence which others.
rows.why: In OPH records are produced in an order all observers share; that order has to become the causal structure of spacetime.

rows.name: Proper time and time dilation
rows.what: Proper time is the time a clock records along its own path; a clock that travels and returns shows less elapsed time.
rows.why: OPH measures time by counting events, so the counts along different paths have to reproduce relativistic time dilation at reunion.

rows.name: Clocks made of events
rows.what: A clock is a physical system whose repeated, countable events let observers compare elapsed time with each other.
rows.why: OPH has no common external clock; its observers read time only from clocks made of records, so every timing prediction rests on them.

rows.name: Smooth continuum fields at large scales
rows.what: At large scales, fields behave as smooth functions on a continuum obeying wave and diffusion equations, despite any underlying discreteness.
rows.why: OPH computes with discrete repair steps; smooth field equations have to emerge as their long-time limit, as heat flow emerges from random walks.

rows.name: Isotropy of propagation
rows.what: Light and particles propagate the same way in every direction; any directional dependence of their dispersion would appear as angular harmonics.
rows.why: OPH builds space from icosahedral cells; their symmetry forbids preferred directions below angular rank six, so low-rank anisotropy would contradict the theory.

rows.name: Propagation anisotropy at l = 6
rows.what: Wave dispersion at very high momentum could depend weakly on direction through an angular rank-six term accompanying the k^4 correction.
rows.why: If icosahedral cells carry propagation, OPH fixes the shape of this term and its ratio to the k^4 term, giving a falsifiable signature.

rows.name: Vacuum birefringence null
rows.what: In vacuum, light of different polarizations travels at the same speed; astrophysical observations bound any polarization-dependent splitting very tightly.
rows.why: A discrete cell structure of space could split polarizations; the null result bounds how OPH's cells may act on light.

rows.name: Relativistic mass shell E^2 = m^2 + p^2
rows.what: A free particle's energy, momentum and rest mass satisfy E^2 = m^2 + p^2 in natural units, the same in every inertial frame.
rows.why: In OPH rest energy and momentum are counted on the same space of observer velocities; this relation links particle kinematics to the Lorentz structure.

rows.name: Mass-energy equivalence (E = mc^2)
rows.what: A body's rest energy equals its mass times the speed of light squared, so internal energy adds to inertia.
rows.why: OPH reads mass as an internal clock rate; the relation then says a system's clock rate is its inertia, linking energy bookkeeping to dynamics.

rows.name: Inverse-square law (Gauss shells)
rows.what: Forces from a point source, such as gravity and electrostatics, weaken as the inverse square of distance in three dimensions.
rows.why: Flux spreading through nested three-dimensional shells gives 1/r^2; reproducing it ties OPH's three spatial directions to the observed force laws.

rows.name: Newtonian mechanics and Lagrangians
rows.what: Classical bodies follow paths that make the action stationary, giving Newton's equations of motion and conserved momenta for each symmetry.
rows.why: OPH has to recover classical mechanics as the stationary-path description of its repair histories, the limit in which everyday motion lives.

rows.name: Force law along worldlines
rows.what: A charged particle's path bends under electric and magnetic fields according to the Lorentz force, which changes its momentum along the worldline.
rows.why: In OPH a force is whatever changes how a charged record is transported along its worldline; this links the gauge field to particle motion.

rows.name: Momentum conservation and covariance
rows.what: The total momentum of a composite system is the sum of its parts and transforms covariantly when the observer changes inertial frame.
rows.why: Collisions and bound systems are described by adding momenta; OPH's momentum bookkeeping has to stay consistent across all observers' frames.

rows.name: Conservation laws and Ward identities
rows.what: Every continuous symmetry of a physical system carries a conserved quantity, such as energy, momentum or charge, with local continuity equations.
rows.why: In OPH each symmetry of the consensus process carries a conserved record; Einstein's equation needs a covariantly conserved matter stress built this way.

rows.name: Proper length
rows.what: Proper length is the distance measured by an observer at rest with the object, for example by timing a light signal's round trip.
rows.why: OPH defines distance through counted record times out and back; reproducing proper length checks that those counts form a consistent spatial geometry.

rows.name: Einstein field equation with Lambda
rows.what: Einstein's equation G_ab + Lambda g_ab = 8 pi G T_ab ties spacetime curvature to the energy and momentum of matter.
rows.why: OPH reads gravity as entropy balance on small light caps seen by overlapping observers; the Einstein equation is where that route has to arrive.

rows.name: Massless graviton
rows.what: The graviton would be the massless spin-two quantum of the gravitational field, with two polarizations matching those of gravitational waves.
rows.why: OPH treats gravity as part of one quantum record theory, so it has to carry massless spin-two excitations matching observed gravitational waves.

rows.name: Bekenstein-Hawking area law
rows.what: A black hole's entropy equals its horizon area divided by four Planck areas, S = A/(4 l_P^2), the Bekenstein-Hawking formula.
rows.why: In OPH entropy counts records crossing a boundary, so it scales with area; matching the coefficient ties record density to the Planck length.

rows.name: Black hole information
rows.what: Information that falls into a black hole appears to be lost, conflicting with unitary quantum evolution unless it returns in the outgoing radiation.
rows.why: OPH stores physics in boundary records shared by observers, so interior information has to stay recoverable from those records.

rows.name: Black-hole ringdown spectrum
rows.what: After two black holes merge, the remnant rings down through damped oscillation modes whose frequencies gravitational-wave detectors measure.
rows.why: If horizons carry discrete record structure, the ringdown spectrum could show extra lines; such lines would test OPH's horizon picture directly.

rows.name: de Sitter time-advance sign
rows.what: In de Sitter space, a shock wave along the cosmological horizon shifts later signals either forward or backward in time, depending on its sign.
rows.why: A finite screen capacity in OPH makes an observer lower the horizon entropy, which fixes the shock's sign as a time advance.

rows.name: Local stress-energy tensor
rows.what: The stress-energy tensor gives the density and flow of energy and momentum at each point, the source term of Einstein's equation.
rows.why: OPH has to build this tensor from how observer records respond on small patches; without it the gravitational route has no source.

rows.name: Equivalence principle (inertial = gravitational mass)
rows.what: All bodies fall with the same acceleration in a gravitational field, because inertial mass equals gravitational mass for every kind of matter.
rows.why: In OPH inertia and gravity would both read one record-level energy ledger; universal free fall is the observable consequence of that identity.

rows.name: Gravitational light deflection
rows.what: Light passing a mass bends by an angle fixed by both the time and space parts of the metric, measured as the PPN parameter gamma.
rows.why: Clock redshift fixes only the time part, so OPH needs independent spatial records or the vacuum Einstein equation to predict light bending.

rows.name: Standard Model gauge algebra su(3)+su(2)+u(1)
rows.what: The Standard Model's forces follow from the gauge symmetry algebra su(3)+su(2)+u(1): colour, weak isospin and hypercharge.
rows.why: OPH reads this algebra from the complete port response of its icosahedral observer cell; obtaining it fixes which forces the theory contains.

rows.name: Global form (SU(3)xSU(2)xU(1))/Z6
rows.what: The Standard Model gauge group can be taken as (SU(3)xSU(2)xU(1))/Z6, because a common Z6 subgroup acts trivially on every known particle.
rows.why: The quotient ties colour, isospin and hypercharge quantization together; OPH's global form decides which charges and representations its matter may carry.

rows.name: Electric charge quantization
rows.what: All observed electric charges are integer multiples of one third of the electron charge, and colour-neutral particles carry whole charges.
rows.why: In OPH charge thirds follow from the gauge group being a quotient by a finite centre, linking charge quantization to the matter content.

rows.name: Colour confinement
rows.what: Quarks and gluons carry colour and never appear in isolation; they are bound into colour-neutral hadrons.
rows.why: OPH has to keep colour SU(3) unbroken and confine coloured states; hadrons and nuclear matter depend on both.

rows.name: Yang-Mills mass gap
rows.what: Pure Yang-Mills theory should have a lightest excitation of strictly positive energy; proving this in four dimensions is a Millennium Prize problem.
rows.why: A gap makes gluonic excitations massive and short-ranged; OPH's account of confinement and of the strong force depends on it.

rows.name: Maxwell's equations
rows.what: Maxwell's equations describe how electric charges and currents produce electric and magnetic fields and how those fields propagate as waves.
rows.why: In OPH electromagnetism is the curvature of port transport around the faces of the observer cell; recovering Maxwell's equations checks that picture.

rows.name: Coulomb's law
rows.what: Two static point charges attract or repel with a force proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to their squared distance.
rows.why: Atomic structure and chemistry rest on this law; OPH has to produce it from minimal static field energy in three dimensions.

rows.name: Charge conservation
rows.what: The total electric charge of an isolated system never changes; charge only moves, with local currents obeying a continuity equation.
rows.why: In OPH charge is a record that moves between ports and is never created or destroyed; gauge invariance of the field equations requires it.

rows.name: Electromagnetic radiation & photons
rows.what: Electromagnetic fields propagate as transverse waves; each wave mode is a quantum harmonic oscillator whose excitations are photons.
rows.why: OPH has to produce light as quantized oscillations of face curvature; most of what observers learn about distant matter arrives this way.

rows.name: No minimal grand unification
rows.what: Minimal grand unified theories such as SU(5) predict X and Y gauge bosons that would mediate proton decay, which experiments have not seen.
rows.why: OPH obtains the Standard Model product group directly, with no X/Y generators, so it predicts no proton decay through that channel.

rows.name: Electroweak symmetry breaking
rows.what: The electroweak symmetry is broken by the Higgs field's vacuum value, giving mass to the W and Z bosons while the photon stays massless.
rows.why: OPH has to reproduce this breaking pattern from its own scalar and gauge structure; weak interactions and particle masses all depend on it.

rows.name: Electroweak hierarchy (why v << M_Planck)
rows.what: The electroweak scale near 246 GeV lies about seventeen orders of magnitude below the Planck scale, a ratio the Standard Model leaves unexplained.
rows.why: OPH would tie this ratio to the capacity of its holographic screen, so the size of the hierarchy follows from screen data.

rows.name: Weak mixing angle
rows.what: The weak mixing angle sets how the neutral electroweak bosons mix into the photon and the Z, measured as sin^2 theta_W near 0.23.
rows.why: OPH would read the angle from gauge kinetic ratios set by its cell geometry, making it a direct test of the gauge sector.

rows.name: Strong coupling alpha_s
rows.what: The strong coupling alpha_s measures the strength of the colour force, conventionally quoted at the Z boson mass, where it is about 0.118.
rows.why: In OPH all couplings would descend from the screen's pixel constant; the strong coupling also enters OPH's fine-structure constant through quark screening.

rows.name: Asymptotic freedom / RG running
rows.what: Gauge couplings change with the energy at which they are probed; the strong coupling weakens at short distances, a property called asymptotic freedom.
rows.why: OPH observers probe at a finite resolution, so the theory has to reproduce how couplings run with that resolution to connect to collider data.

rows.name: Holonomy and Aharonov-Bohm phases
rows.what: A charged particle taken around a closed loop picks up a phase set by the enclosed flux, even where the local field vanishes.
rows.why: Gauge fields act through loop phases; OPH observers have to see such path-dependent phases in their records for its gauge forces to be physical.

rows.name: Arrow of time
rows.what: Macroscopic processes run in one direction: entropy grows, records accumulate, and observers remember only the past.
rows.why: In OPH repair removes disagreements and does not recreate them, so the direction in which records accumulate is the time direction observers read.

rows.name: Zeroth law (temperature)
rows.what: Two bodies each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other, which defines a common temperature.
rows.why: In OPH temperature is a shared modular reference on a common boundary; thermometry and all thermodynamic predictions start from it.

rows.name: First law (energy conservation)
rows.what: Energy is conserved: the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added minus the work it does.
rows.why: OPH defines energy as the modular generator of repair, additive over independent patches; heat, work and gravity all use this ledger.

rows.name: Second law (entropy increase)
rows.what: The entropy of an isolated system never decreases, and spontaneous processes move systems toward equilibrium.
rows.why: In OPH consensus repair removes disagreement, so entropy relative to equilibrium cannot decrease; this links thermodynamics to the record dynamics itself.

rows.name: Third law
rows.what: As temperature approaches absolute zero, entropy approaches a minimum, and no finite process can cool a system all the way to zero.
rows.why: In OPH reaching zero temperature would take unbounded repair resources; low-temperature behaviour tests how records settle into ground states.

rows.name: Landauer bound
rows.what: Erasing one bit of information dissipates at least kT ln 2 of heat into the environment.
rows.why: OPH treats records as physical, so forgetting one is a physical act with a minimum energy price fixed by temperature.

rows.name: Fluctuation relations
rows.what: In small systems entropy can briefly decrease, and the odds of a history versus its time reverse grow exponentially with entropy production.
rows.why: OPH's repair histories have to obey these exact identities, which make the second law a statistical statement about record trajectories.

rows.name: Transport, diffusion and Green-Kubo
rows.what: Transport coefficients such as diffusion constants and conductivities equal time integrals of equilibrium current correlations, the Green-Kubo relations.
rows.why: OPH has to get macroscopic diffusion and conduction from correlations of its microscopic repair currents, linking record dynamics to measurable transport.

rows.name: Work and response
rows.what: Work and pressure measure how a system's energy responds to a change of its volume or other external parameters.
rows.why: Energy records at one volume leave pressure undetermined, so in OPH work and heat depend on an explicit description of the volume change.

rows.name: Up quark and antiquark (u, ū)
rows.what: The up quark has charge +2/3 and spin 1/2 and is confined in protons, neutrons and other hadrons; its antiquark carries the opposite charges.
rows.why: OPH reads particles as defects of the record process; protons and neutrons need an up-type defect carrying charge +2/3, colour and spin half.

rows.name: Down quark and antiquark (d, d̄)
rows.what: The down quark has charge -1/3 and spin 1/2 and builds protons and neutrons with the up quark; its antiquark carries the opposite charges.
rows.why: OPH has to produce a second colour-carrying defect with charge -1/3; the proton-neutron difference and beta decay rest on it.

rows.name: Strange quark and antiquark (s, s̄)
rows.what: The strange quark is the second-generation down-type quark with charge -1/3, found with its antiquark in kaons and hyperons.
rows.why: OPH's defect classes carry charge but no generation label, so telling strange from down needs a flavour discriminator, a test of family structure.

rows.name: Charm quark and antiquark (c, c̄)
rows.what: The charm quark is the second-generation up-type quark with charge +2/3, identified with its antiquark in D mesons and charmonium.
rows.why: OPH has to account for a heavier copy of the up quark; its existence tests how the theory produces three quark generations.

rows.name: Bottom quark and antiquark (b, b̄)
rows.what: The bottom quark is the third-generation down-type quark with charge -1/3, observed with its antiquark in B hadrons and their weak decays.
rows.why: OPH has to produce a third down-type family member; B-hadron decays carry much of the measured CP violation and quark mixing.

rows.name: Top quark and antiquark (t, t̄)
rows.what: The top quark, charge +2/3, is the heaviest known elementary particle; colliders produce it with its antiquark in pairs that decay through W bosons.
rows.why: OPH has to place a third up-type defect whose large Higgs coupling shapes the stability of the electroweak vacuum.

rows.name: Electron and positron (e⁻, e⁺)
rows.what: The electron is the stable lightest charged lepton with charge -1 and spin 1/2; the positron is its antiparticle with charge +1.
rows.why: Atoms, chemistry and electrical currents run on the electron; OPH has to produce a defect with its charge, field, spin and weak response together.

rows.name: Muon and antimuon (μ⁻, μ⁺)
rows.what: The muon is an unstable heavier copy of the electron with the same charge and spin; the antimuon is its antiparticle with charge +1.
rows.why: OPH's defect classes carry no generation label, so a distinct muon branch with its own decay tests how the theory produces lepton families.

rows.name: Tau and antitau (τ⁻, τ⁺)
rows.what: The tau is the third and heaviest charged lepton, decaying weakly into leptons or hadrons; the antitau is its antiparticle with charge +1.
rows.why: A third charged-lepton branch tests whether OPH produces exactly three lepton generations, each with its own weak decay channels.

rows.name: Electron neutrino and antineutrino (νe, ν̄e)
rows.what: The electron neutrino and its antineutrino are neutral spin-1/2 leptons produced and detected with electrons and positrons, as in beta decay.
rows.why: OPH has to produce a neutral weak partner of the electron; oscillations show these flavour states mix massive states, testing its flavour sector.

rows.name: Muon neutrino and antineutrino (νμ, ν̄μ)
rows.what: The muon neutrino and its antineutrino are neutral spin-1/2 leptons produced and detected with muons, for example in pion decays.
rows.why: OPH has to give each lepton family its own neutral partner; muon-neutrino beams measure the large atmospheric mixing the theory must reproduce.

rows.name: Tau neutrino and antineutrino (ντ, ν̄τ)
rows.what: The tau neutrino and its antineutrino are neutral spin-1/2 leptons produced and detected together with tau leptons.
rows.why: A third neutral lepton completes the family pattern OPH has to reproduce; three light neutrinos match the measured invisible width of the Z.

rows.name: Photon (γ)
rows.what: The photon is the massless quantum of light, carrying energy, momentum and two polarizations, and coupling to electric charge.
rows.why: OPH has to produce photons as discrete quanta of a transverse field coupled to its charges; all optical observation relies on them.

rows.name: Gluons (g, 8 colour states)
rows.what: Gluons are the eight massless carriers of the strong force, carrying colour themselves and binding quarks into hadrons.
rows.why: OPH's colour symmetry has eight generators; realizing them as confined vector quanta tests its strong sector against three-jet events and scaling violations.

rows.name: W bosons (W⁺, W⁻)
rows.what: The W bosons are the massive charged carriers of the weak force, a conjugate pair mediating charged-current processes such as beta decay.
rows.why: In OPH the charged weak directions shift a doublet's charge by one unit; producing them as particles tests its electroweak sector.

rows.name: Z boson
rows.what: The Z boson is the massive, neutral carrier of the weak force, coupling to every fermion through neutral currents.
rows.why: In OPH the form of the Z couplings follows from the electroweak structure; precise Z line-shape and coupling measurements test it directly.

rows.name: Higgs boson (H)
rows.what: The Higgs boson is the neutral, spin-zero excitation of the field that breaks electroweak symmetry, with couplings growing with particle mass.
rows.why: Electroweak breaking in OPH leaves one radial scalar direction; observing it as a resonance with the measured couplings tests the scalar sector.

rows.name: Proton and antiproton (p, p̄)
rows.what: The proton is the stable positive baryon of two up quarks and one down quark; the antiproton is its conjugate with charge -1.
rows.why: OPH has to bind three colour-carrying defects into a stable colour singlet with charge +1 and spin half; every atomic nucleus depends on it.

rows.name: Neutron and antineutron (n, n̄)
rows.what: The neutron is the neutral baryon of one up and two down quarks, beta-decaying when free; the antineutron carries opposite baryon number.
rows.why: Nuclei need both nucleons; OPH has to distinguish the neutral composite from the proton and produce its beta decay into a proton, electron and antineutrino.

rows.name: Pions (π⁺, π⁰, π⁻)
rows.what: Pions are the lightest hadrons, spin-zero quark-antiquark states with charges +1, 0 and -1, which carry the long-range part of the nuclear force.
rows.why: OPH has to bind quark and antiquark defects into colour singlets with pion quantum numbers, the first test of its meson sector.

rows.name: Other hadrons (kaons, hyperons, mesons, resonances)
rows.what: Hundreds of further hadrons, including kaons, hyperons, heavier mesons and short-lived resonances, form the measured spectrum of strongly bound states.
rows.why: OPH has to tell elementary channels, composites and resonances apart from complete records; the full hadron spectrum tests its strong sector broadly.

rows.name: Higgs boson mass
rows.what: The Higgs boson mass is the rest energy of the electroweak scalar particle; it fixes the strength of the Higgs self-coupling.
rows.why: The Higgs mass ties OPH's scalar sector to measurement and, with the top mass, decides whether the electroweak vacuum is stable.

rows.name: Top quark pole mass
rows.what: The top quark pole mass is the rest energy of the heaviest known elementary particle, whose Higgs coupling is close to one.
rows.why: The top mass sets the largest Yukawa coupling, so any OPH account of fermion masses and vacuum stability has to reproduce it.

rows.name: W boson mass
rows.what: The W boson mass is the rest energy of the charged weak boson, set by the weak coupling and the Higgs vacuum value.
rows.why: The W-to-Z mass ratio tests OPH's electroweak breaking and the radiative corrections linking its gauge sector to precision data.

rows.name: Z boson mass
rows.what: The Z boson mass is the rest energy of the neutral weak boson, measured with very high precision from the Z resonance line shape.
rows.why: The Z mass anchors the electroweak precision fit, so every comparison of OPH's electroweak sector with data runs through it.

rows.name: Koide relation Q = 2/3
rows.what: The Koide ratio (m_e + m_mu + m_tau)/(sqrt m_e + sqrt m_mu + sqrt m_tau)^2 equals 2/3 within measurement precision for the charged leptons.
rows.why: The relation has no Standard Model explanation; OPH links it to a balanced three-state circulant structure, which a precise tau mass measurement can test.

rows.name: Tau lepton mass
rows.what: The tau mass is the rest energy of the heaviest charged lepton, measured from the production threshold in electron-positron collisions.
rows.why: A tau mass measurement at higher precision decides a registered OPH test of the balance premise behind the Koide relation.

rows.name: Electron mass
rows.what: The electron mass is the rest energy of the lightest charged lepton; it sets the size of atoms and the energy scale of chemistry.
rows.why: The electron's rest energy links OPH's internal clock units to atomic physics, where measurements are most precise.

rows.name: Muon mass
rows.what: The muon mass is the rest energy of the second-generation charged lepton, roughly two hundred times the electron mass.
rows.why: The Standard Model leaves the lepton mass hierarchy unexplained; it is a central test of how OPH produces fermion families.

rows.name: Absolute quark masses
rows.what: The six quark masses, from the light up and down to the heavy top, span about five orders of magnitude.
rows.why: Quark masses set hadron properties and, through the top, vacuum stability; they test whether OPH's flavour sector fixes the Yukawa couplings.

rows.name: Strange-to-down quark mass ratio
rows.what: The ratio of strange to down quark masses, about 20 in lattice QCD, is a scale-independent measure of light-quark flavour structure.
rows.why: Being dimensionless, the ratio tests any OPH light-quark flavour law without needing an absolute mass scale.

rows.name: Cabibbo angle and CKM mixing
rows.what: The Cabibbo angle measures how strongly weak interactions mix down and strange quarks, the leading off-diagonal entry of the CKM matrix.
rows.why: Quark mixing governs flavour-changing weak decays; OPH has to obtain it from the quark Yukawa matrices, which icosahedral geometry alone does not fix.

rows.name: CP violation phase
rows.what: The CP-violating phase of quark mixing makes matter and antimatter decay differently, measured in kaon and B-meson decays through the Jarlskog invariant.
rows.why: CP violation is one condition for a matter excess; OPH needs a rule that supplies a complex orientation, since real inputs give no CP phase.

rows.name: Neutrino mixing (PMNS)
rows.what: Neutrinos produced in one flavour oscillate into others because flavour states mix mass states, described by the PMNS matrix with two large angles.
rows.why: The contrast between large lepton mixing and small quark mixing is a sharp test for OPH's flavour sector and its conserved defect labels.

rows.name: Neutrino mass ordering
rows.what: The neutrino mass ordering is whether the third mass state is heavier (normal) or lighter (inverted) than the other two.
rows.why: The ordering is a binary question that JUNO, DUNE and Hyper-Kamiokande will settle, making it a clean advance test of OPH's neutrino sector.

rows.name: Absolute neutrino masses
rows.what: Absolute neutrino masses are the rest energies of the three neutrino mass states, known to be nonzero and well below one electronvolt.
rows.why: Neutrino masses lie outside the minimal Standard Model, so their origin tests whether OPH's matter sector includes a mass mechanism beyond it.

rows.name: Nucleon and proton mass
rows.what: The proton mass is the rest energy of the proton, arising almost entirely from QCD binding energy, with quark masses contributing a few percent.
rows.why: Because the proton mass is strong-interaction energy, reproducing it tests OPH's colour binding and strong coupling directly.

rows.name: Hadron spectrum
rows.what: The hadron spectrum is the full set of measured meson and baryon masses, which QCD fixes from a few quark masses and one coupling.
rows.why: The spectrum tests OPH's strong sector as a whole: binding, confinement, flavour and the coupling all enter every state.

rows.name: Baryon-number violation and proton stability
rows.what: Baryon number counts quarks minus antiquarks in thirds; its violation would allow proton decay and could explain the universe's excess of matter over antimatter.
rows.why: Proton lifetime limits and the observed matter excess both constrain which baryon-violating operators OPH's matter content and gauge group allow.

rows.name: One anomaly-free generation of 15 Weyl states
rows.what: Each Standard Model generation consists of fifteen chiral Weyl states with fixed colour, weak and hypercharge quantum numbers, free of gauge anomalies.
rows.why: OPH selects this multiplet from its five-level code by chirality and anomaly cancellation; reproducing it is a basic test of its account of matter.

rows.name: Parity violation and chirality
rows.what: The weak interaction acts only on left-handed fermions, so the laws of physics distinguish left from right and violate mirror symmetry.
rows.why: OPH has to produce a left-right asymmetric generation from its selection rules; chirality fixes which fermions feel the weak force.

rows.name: Three generations
rows.what: Quarks and leptons come in three families with identical charges and different masses, and the Z boson width counts three light neutrinos.
rows.why: The Standard Model leaves the number of families unexplained; OPH relates it to the three-dimensional slowest band of its screen cell.

rows.name: Yukawa couplings
rows.what: Yukawa couplings link fermions to the Higgs field and set the charged-fermion masses and the quark mixing matrix, spanning about six orders of magnitude.
rows.why: Gauge symmetry leaves the three Yukawa matrices free, so OPH needs an interaction rule that fixes them to account for fermion masses and mixing.

rows.name: Standard Model action
rows.what: The Standard Model action combines gauge kinetic terms, the Higgs potential, fermion kinetic terms and Yukawa couplings into one Lagrangian for non-gravitational physics.
rows.why: A complete theory must produce every term and coefficient of this action from one source; it is the central matter target for OPH.

rows.name: Unitary scattering
rows.what: Particles approach, interact and separate, and a unitary S-matrix maps incoming to outgoing states, giving the cross sections measured at colliders.
rows.why: Collider data are scattering data; OPH needs asymptotic states and an S-matrix built from its finite unitary updates to compare with them.

rows.name: Vacuum stability under time evolution
rows.what: The vacuum is the stable empty state of a quantum field; time evolution should leave it empty and create no spurious particles or energy.
rows.why: OPH evolves fields in discrete steps, so it has to keep the vacuum stable to the precision observers find while excitations propagate.

rows.name: Charged Weyl fermions
rows.what: Massless charged fermions propagate as Weyl particles of fixed handedness at the speed of light.
rows.why: OPH's discrete matter account has to reproduce Weyl propagation and control fermion doubling, the unwanted extra species a lattice produces.

rows.name: Fine-structure constant 1/alpha
rows.what: The fine-structure constant alpha, about 1/137, is the dimensionless strength of electromagnetism, measured to better than a part per billion.
rows.why: A value from the screen geometry would tie a measured coupling constant to the observer carrier and test OPH at extreme precision.

rows.name: Cosmological constant magnitude
rows.what: The cosmological constant Lambda drives the late-time acceleration of cosmic expansion; its value is about 10⁻¹²² in Planck units.
rows.why: OPH reads Lambda in Planck units as 3 pi/N for a record capacity N, so its tiny value would reflect a huge count of records.

rows.name: Scale-invariant primordial fluctuations (Harrison-Zel'dovich)
rows.what: Primordial curvature fluctuations carry nearly equal power on every length scale, the Harrison-Zel'dovich spectrum seen in the CMB and galaxy distribution.
rows.why: OPH proposes that maximum-entropy screen statistics give this spectrum without an inflaton field, which would replace a central role of inflation.

rows.name: Scalar spectral tilt n_s
rows.what: The scalar spectral tilt n_s measures how primordial fluctuation power changes with scale; measured values lie slightly below one.
rows.why: OPH proposes n_s = 1 - P/48, which ties the early Universe to the same pixel constant that enters the gauge couplings.

rows.name: FLRW expansion
rows.what: On large scales the Universe is homogeneous and isotropic, and its expansion is described by one scale factor that grows with cosmic time.
rows.why: OPH reads the scale factor as a density of records per comoving cell and tick, so expansion has to emerge from record counts.

rows.name: Icosahedral pattern in the large-angle CMB
rows.what: The large-angle CMB sky may carry a pattern with icosahedral A5 symmetry, whose first nonconstant invariant multipole is l = 6.
rows.why: An icosahedral pattern in the large-angle CMB would be a direct imprint of the screen symmetry on the sky.

rows.name: Structure formation
rows.what: Galaxies and clusters grow from small primordial fluctuations under gravity, measured by the matter power spectrum and the growth rate of structure.
rows.why: Matter power and growth rate test any proposed source of primordial fluctuations and any dark component OPH adds.

rows.name: Hubble constant value
rows.what: The Hubble constant H0 is the present expansion rate of the Universe, the recession speed per unit distance of nearby galaxies.
rows.why: Local and CMB-based determinations of H0 disagree, so a value from OPH's record clocks would bear on the Hubble tension.

rows.name: Initial state / big bang
rows.what: Observers read a hot, dense early phase of the Universe from the CMB and light-element abundances.
rows.why: OPH has no external initial time, so it has to produce this early record history without a time before the history.

rows.name: Running of the scalar spectral tilt
rows.what: The running of the tilt measures how the spectral index n_s itself changes with scale.
rows.why: A single source dilation in OPH gives a pure power law with zero running, which future CMB data can test.

rows.name: Primordial gravitational waves (tensor-to-scalar ratio r)
rows.what: The tensor-to-scalar ratio r measures primordial gravitational waves relative to density fluctuations; inflation generically predicts a nonzero value.
rows.why: OPH's inflation-free branch has no tensor source and predicts r = 0, so a detected primordial gravitational-wave background would refute it.

rows.name: Primordial isocurvature fluctuations
rows.what: Isocurvature fluctuations change the relative abundances of species without changing total curvature; observations find primordial perturbations to be adiabatic.
rows.why: OPH's single release clock for all species leaves only adiabatic perturbations, a prediction shared with the standard cosmological model.

rows.name: Primordial non-Gaussianity f_NL
rows.what: f_NL measures how far primordial fluctuations depart from Gaussian statistics through their three-point correlation.
rows.why: OPH's maximum-entropy screen law is Gaussian at the source, so non-Gaussianity separates its single-clock origin from multi-field alternatives.

rows.name: Spatial curvature Ω_K
rows.what: Omega_K measures the spatial curvature of the Universe; observations find space flat to better than a percent.
rows.why: Flatness is usually attributed to inflation; OPH's branch gives zero curvature without it, and a confirmed nonzero value would refute that branch.

rows.name: Cosmological redshift
rows.what: Cosmological redshift stretches light from distant sources by the ratio of the scale factors at reception and emission.
rows.why: Redshift is the main record of cosmic expansion; OPH reads it from ratios of record counts without an external clock.

rows.name: Horizon-scale uniformity of the early Universe
rows.what: The CMB has nearly the same temperature across regions that expansion without an inflationary phase would never have brought into causal contact.
rows.why: OPH has to explain this coherence, together with flatness and scale invariance, through one common clock on the observer screen without an inflaton.

rows.name: CMB acoustic peaks (photon-baryon fluid)
rows.what: Photons and baryons oscillate as one fluid before recombination, producing the acoustic peaks in the CMB temperature and polarization spectra.
rows.why: Once the source and photons are given, standard transport yields the peaks; OPH must supply both on one process to predict them.

rows.name: Sum of neutrino masses Σm_ν
rows.what: The sum of the three neutrino masses suppresses small-scale clustering of matter and is bounded by cosmological data.
rows.why: A theory of the particle content has to keep the summed neutrino mass below cosmological bounds; it links particle physics to structure growth.

rows.name: Relativistic species N_eff
rows.what: N_eff counts the effective number of relativistic species, such as neutrinos, in the early Universe.
rows.why: It tests the particle content together with its thermal history, both of which OPH has to produce on one process.

rows.name: Baryon-to-photon ratio η_b
rows.what: The baryon-to-photon ratio, about six parts in ten billion, measures how much matter outnumbers antimatter in the Universe.
rows.why: OPH must produce this excess from its records, which needs a symmetry-breaking source and a record dictionary for baryon number.

rows.name: Dark-matter density Ω_c h²
rows.what: Omega_c h² is the present density of cold dark matter, which fixes the CMB peak heights and the growth of structure.
rows.why: OPH proposes conserved collar charge as dark matter, so its abundance has to match this density from one physical source.

rows.name: Big Bang nucleosynthesis (light-element abundances)
rows.what: In the first minutes, nuclear reactions fixed the helium, deuterium and lithium fractions observed in primordial gas.
rows.why: Light-element abundances test the early thermal history, expansion rate and nuclear sector that OPH has to produce on one process.

rows.name: CMB temperature today
rows.what: The CMB has a blackbody temperature of about 2.725 kelvin today, which fixes the present photon density.
rows.why: The temperature anchors the thermal history; OPH needs a photon sector and a physical scale to produce it.

rows.name: Dark matter
rows.what: Galaxies, lensing and cosmic structure require more gravitating mass than luminous matter provides; the unseen component is called dark matter.
rows.why: OPH proposes that gravity counts records that never couple to light, so dark matter would be non-luminous modular charge.

rows.name: Flat rotation curves & baryonic Tully-Fisher
rows.what: Outer rotation speeds of disk galaxies stay flat, and their fourth power scales with the galaxy's baryonic mass.
rows.why: The deep-regime law g = sqrt(g_bar a0) gives both, so these curves test OPH's collar account of the dark sector.

rows.name: Acceleration scale a0
rows.what: The acceleration scale a0 marks where galaxy dynamics depart from Newtonian gravity of the visible mass, at about 10⁻¹⁰ m/s².
rows.why: a0 is the only scale in OPH's deep-regime law, so a source value would turn rotation-curve fits into a prediction.

rows.name: Scatter of the radial acceleration relation
rows.what: The radial acceleration relation ties observed to baryonic acceleration in galaxies with very small scatter around one curve.
rows.why: A source of the dark-sector signal should also fix how far individual galaxies scatter, a sharper test than the mean relation.

rows.name: Gravitational lensing by dark matter
rows.what: Gravitational lensing measures the total mass along light paths through the bending of light around galaxies and clusters.
rows.why: A dark-sector source has to bend light consistently with the orbital speeds it explains, which tests OPH's collar charge as one source.

rows.name: Dark-energy equation of state w
rows.what: The dark-energy equation of state w is pressure over density; a cosmological constant has w = -1 and no evolution.
rows.why: Fixed record capacity in OPH forces w = -1, so the evolving dark energy hinted by DESI tests the capacity reading.

rows.name: Integer electric charge of free particles
rows.what: Every free electric charge ever measured is an integer multiple of the elementary charge e.
rows.why: A recovery has to produce the unit charge from the dynamics and forbid splitting one unit into two half charges.

rows.name: Electron rest energy
rows.what: The electron's rest energy is the energy equivalent of its mass and anchors the energy scale of the charged-lepton sector.
rows.why: A recovery must select the electron state dynamically and let its energy fix a second, independently measured quantity such as inertia.

rows.name: de Broglie internal clock at the rest-energy frequency
rows.what: Quantum mechanics assigns every massive particle an internal clock ticking at its rest energy divided by Planck's constant.
rows.why: A wave model of matter has to produce this internal clock on the same state whose rest energy is measured.

rows.name: Particle stability under free evolution
rows.what: Particles persist under free evolution, while localized configurations in many classical field theories collapse or disperse, as Derrick's theorem shows.
rows.why: A wave model of matter has to escape Derrick-type collapse or dispersal before any of its excitations can count as particles.

rows.name: Electron magnetic moment (g ≈ 2)
rows.what: The electron carries a magnetic dipole moment with g close to 2 and precesses in an applied magnetic field.
rows.why: A model has to source this dipole from the particle's own circulation and reproduce the measured g factor.

rows.name: Electron spin angular momentum ħ/2
rows.what: The electron carries intrinsic spin angular momentum of magnitude hbar/2.
rows.why: A field model has to show this angular momentum in the field of the same electron state.

rows.name: Spin-½ sign under 360° rotation and exchange
rows.what: Fermions change sign under a full 360-degree rotation and under exchange, returning to themselves only after 720 degrees.
rows.why: This sign underlies the Pauli exclusion principle and atomic structure, so a model of matter has to produce it.

rows.name: Antiparticles and annihilation into radiation
rows.what: Every charged particle has an antiparticle with which it annihilates into radiation, as in positronium decay to two or three photons.
rows.why: Producing conjugate pairs that annihilate into radiation quanta tests whether a model's matter carries charge conjugation and couples to light.

rows.name: Light neutral decay products (neutrinos)
rows.what: Neutrinos are light, electrically neutral particles released in weak decays.
rows.why: A model of matter has to produce such light neutral states among decay products to recover the weak sector.

rows.name: Neutrino flavour oscillations (PMNS)
rows.what: Neutrinos are produced in one of three flavours and oscillate between flavours in flight, governed by the PMNS mixing matrix.
rows.why: Oscillations show that neutrinos have mass and mix, so a theory of the particle content has to reproduce the measured mixing angles.

rows.name: Charged-lepton spectrum (electron, muon, tau)
rows.what: The electron, muon and tau share one charge and spin and form three charged-lepton species with widely separated rest energies.
rows.why: A recovery has to produce exactly three charged species from one dynamics, with consistent recoil and formation energies for each.

rows.name: Fractional quark charges
rows.what: Quarks carry fractional electric charges of -1/3 and +2/3 of the elementary charge.
rows.why: A model has to produce fractional charge, for instance as a fractional winding, and match it against an independent electric standard.

rows.name: Baryons as bound states of three quarks
rows.what: Protons and neutrons are stable bound states of three quarks held together by the strong force.
rows.why: A model has to bind three constituents against every fragmentation channel and show they are quarks with charge and colour.

rows.name: Neutron-proton mass ordering and nucleon charge profiles
rows.what: The neutron is slightly heavier than the proton and has a positive core with a negative outer charge distribution.
rows.why: The mass ordering and charge profile test whether a model distinguishes proton and neutron states with physical detectors.

rows.name: Proton and neutron rest energies
rows.what: The proton and neutron rest energies are measured to better than a part per billion.
rows.why: Their precision makes them a sharp target for any field-based prediction of hadron masses from one common law.

rows.name: Deuteron binding and quadrupole moment
rows.what: The deuteron, a proton bound to a neutron by about 2.2 MeV, has a small electric quadrupole moment.
rows.why: The quadrupole moment reveals the tensor part of the nuclear force, which a model of nuclei has to reproduce.

rows.name: Nuclear binding, excitation levels and halo nuclei
rows.what: Nuclei have measured binding energies, excitation levels and, for halo nuclei, extended neutron clouds with measured lifetimes.
rows.why: Nuclear structure tests whether a model's hadrons bind into the many nuclear species with their observed spectra.

rows.name: Pions, kaons and strange decays
rows.what: Pions and kaons are the lightest quark-antiquark bound states, and strange hadrons decay weakly with a change of strangeness.
rows.why: Mesons test whether a model binds quark-antiquark pairs and carries the flavour quantum numbers seen in weak decays.

rows.name: Stable neutral massive excitation (dark-matter candidate)
rows.what: A dark-matter particle would be a stable, electrically neutral, massive excitation that emits no light.
rows.why: Gravitational observations need such a component, and a stable neutral bound state in the model would be a candidate.

rows.name: Coulomb 1/r potential of an elementary charge
rows.what: Two static charges interact through a potential that falls as 1/r, with a strength set by alpha.
rows.why: A recovery has to produce the inverse-distance law from one elementary charge and derive its strength from the mechanism.

rows.name: Lorentz covariance and a limiting signal speed
rows.what: Physics has no preferred inertial frame: moving clocks slow, moving bodies contract and no signal outruns the speed of light.
rows.why: OPH starts from a discrete network, so it has to produce frame-free boost behaviour and one limiting speed for all excitations.

rows.name: Linear confinement of colour charges
rows.what: Quarks are confined by a potential that grows linearly with separation, with a string tension of about 1 GeV/fm.
rows.why: Confinement explains why free quarks are never seen, so a model has to produce a linear potential between identified colour charges.

rows.name: Scale-dependent (running) coupling
rows.what: Measured couplings change with the energy scale of the probe, with structure that sets in at the size of the scatterer.
rows.why: Running couplings are central to gauge theories, so a model has to identify its scale-dependent interaction with a physical gauge coupling.

rows.name: Muon decay
rows.what: The muon decays into an electron and two neutrinos with a mean lifetime of about 2.2 microseconds.
rows.why: Muon decay is the cleanest weak process and fixes the Fermi constant, so a model has to reproduce it on identified states.

rows.name: Neutron beta decay and parity violation
rows.what: A free neutron decays into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino, and the decay violates parity.
rows.why: Beta decay ties the weak force to nuclear matter, so a model has to produce the tagged decay and its parity asymmetry.

rows.name: Newtonian inverse-square gravity between masses
rows.what: Masses attract with an inverse-square force of strength G, the Newtonian limit of general relativity.
rows.why: A recovery has to produce attraction between independent masses and derive Newton's constant from the mechanism.

rows.name: Light bending, gravitational redshift and Shapiro delay
rows.what: Gravity bends light, slows clocks and delays signals, observed as light deflection, gravitational redshift and Shapiro delay.
rows.why: These effects test whether a source curves spacetime for clocks and light together, as general relativity requires.

rows.name: Accelerating cosmic expansion
rows.what: Distant supernovae and the CMB show that cosmic expansion accelerates, consistent with a small positive cosmological constant.
rows.why: Its tiny value is the largest unexplained number in physics, and OPH relates it to the total record capacity.

rows.name: Transverse electromagnetic waves (Maxwell)
rows.what: Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave obeying Maxwell's equations and travelling at the speed of light.
rows.why: A model has to produce a propagating mode with electric and magnetic readouts, two transverse polarizations and one limiting speed.

rows.name: Klein-Gordon dispersion of matter waves
rows.what: Free matter waves obey the Klein-Gordon relation, frequency squared equals wave number squared plus mass squared in natural units.
rows.why: Recovering this relation with independently measured space and time observables shows that a model's excitations behave as relativistic matter.

rows.name: Hydrogen-like orbital energy levels
rows.what: Atoms have discrete standing-wave energy levels, with hydrogen's levels spaced as 1/n².
rows.why: Discrete levels with the hydrogenic spacing test whether a model's bound states reproduce atomic structure.

rows.name: Colour deconfinement transition
rows.what: Pure SU(3) gauge theory confines colour at low temperature and becomes deconfined through a first-order transition at high temperature.
rows.why: Confinement and deconfinement are defining nonperturbative features of the colour force, so OPH's seam cost has to reproduce them.

rows.name: Why is there anything rather than nothing?
rows.what: This asks why any universe exists at all rather than nothing, a question that seems to need a cause before every cause.
rows.why: OPH proposes to end the regress with a self-reading Universe U whose recovered account D(U), realized inside it, gives back U: R(D(U)) ≅ U.

rows.name: Why is there subjective experience (qualia)?
rows.what: Subjective experience is the qualitative, lived character of perception and thought, beyond what any public record of it carries.
rows.why: OPH takes observers as primitive, so it has to say where experience enters its account of records and readouts.

rows.name: Why exactly these laws and constants?
rows.what: This asks why nature follows these particular laws and constants among all conceivable ones.
rows.why: Physics takes its laws and constants as given, while a closed self-reading universe would have to account for them from inside.

rows.name: Relativistic QFT as effective description
rows.what: Relativistic quantum field theory describes particles as excitations of local fields consistent with special relativity and causality.
rows.why: In OPH fields describe what observers jointly measure, so relativistic QFT must emerge as the description of agreed records at accessible scales.

rows.name: confluent terminating repair contract
rows.what: Local repair moves fix every covered mismatch, overlapping repairs reconcile to a common result, and every accepted repair strictly lowers a well-founded measure.
rows.why: It makes repair terminate and lets observers with equal protected readings reach the same final records whatever the order of repairs.
rows.statement: Declared repair moves close every covered local mismatch, overlapping moves complete to a common local diamond on the protected observation quotient, and every accepted nontrivial transaction strictly lowers one declared well-founded measure. Normal endpoints from sources with equal protected observation then agree exactly when the observation identifies consistent states.

rows.name: algebra-state representation of public records
rows.what: Public records are mutually orthogonal projectors in a finite complex matrix algebra, and states are read out through the trace.
rows.why: It places records in the standard quantum framework, so OPH's finite theorems on measurement, probability and locality use matrix algebra.
rows.statement: Public records are the span of the mutually orthogonal projectors of a projective partition inside a finite complex matrix star algebra. States are read through the trace pairing, and record events use that algebraic readout.

rows.name: operational effect additivity
rows.what: Probabilities of compatible measurement outcomes add: the value of a combined outcome equals the sum of its parts in every measurement context.
rows.why: With it a finite Gleason-type theorem forces the Born rule, the squared-amplitude form of quantum probabilities.
rows.statement: A public frame valuation is additive on every required coexistent effect sum, v(A + B) = v(A) + v(B) whenever A + B is an effect, across measurement contexts. With it the finite Busch-Gleason theorem forces the Born trace form.

rows.name: declared phase-sensitive effect
rows.what: One specific phase-sensitive measurement outcome, the projector onto the plus eigenstate of Pauli Y, is declared as part of the measurement set.
rows.why: Together with two real-valued effects it completes state tomography of a two-level system, so complex quantum phase becomes testable.
rows.statement: The matrix I/2 - (2*sqrt(3)/3)*i*(QP - PQ), the Pauli-Y plus projector (I+Y)/2, is one declared phase-sensitive effect; with the two committed real effects it completes fixed-trace two-by-two tomography. The declaration supplies an effect only, not an instrument.

rows.name: counting path reference
rows.what: The reference weighting of histories is a given initial distribution times equal weight for every transition step.
rows.why: OPH's state-selection principle measures every candidate law against this reference, the unique choice treating all transition targets alike.
rows.statement: The path-space reference is a supplied initial law times the uniform-step counting weight. Axiom 3 takes this reference as an input; among row-stochastic kernels it is characterized by invariance under relabeling of transition targets at fixed source.

rows.name: real Legendre enrichment
rows.what: Extending the finite transition rule to a real-valued Lagrangian requires choosing one velocity curvature, a choice invisible in every realized history.
rows.why: The choice fixes which classical Hamiltonian mechanics OPH attaches to its histories, since different values give different Legendre-Hamilton systems.
rows.statement: The finite source law fixes its four-corner log-transition action and a bilinear real extension affine in the velocity slot; selecting one real velocity curvature a in L_a = L_0 + (a/2)y(y-1) is a representation choice, since every a > 0 leaves all realized histories unchanged and gives different Legendre-Hamilton systems.

rows.name: common reference for state and transition selection
rows.what: State selection and transition selection share one faithful reference, and transitions resample among states agreeing with the full repaired visible record.
rows.why: From these inputs OPH derives Gibbs states and weighted resampling from one source, giving a finite form of the four thermodynamic laws.
rows.statement: One common faithful reference serves both Axiom 3 instantiations, and the transition feasible set is the fibre of the complete repaired visible datum of the active collar. On these inputs the state projection selects the Gibbs family and the transition projection selects weighted conditional resampling from the same reference, giving the finite four-law package.

rows.name: refinement-uniform low-temperature control
rows.what: Across a family of regulated models, one bound drives the weight away from the ground state to zero at low temperature, with a common threshold.
rows.why: It is needed to carry finite thermodynamic statements over to statements uniform under refinement and in the continuum limit.
rows.statement: A declared indexed regulator family carries one uniform low-temperature tail bound that drives the off-minimum Gibbs mass, and where claimed the entropy excess, to zero with one inverse-temperature threshold across the family. It is needed for regulator-uniform and continuum statements, not for the finite four-law clauses.

rows.name: equal-face-weight and barycentric one-third port-dual rules
rows.what: Each of the twenty faces of the carrier gets equal weight, and each face shares its weight equally among its three ports.
rows.why: The resulting measure gives every port weight one twelfth and defines the metric OPH uses to classify the gauge symmetry type.
rows.statement: The port-dual measure places equal normalized weights on the twenty faces of the oriented carrier and shares each face weight one third to each incident port, giving port weight 1/12.

rows.name: port-weight metric and nearest compact-family verdict
rows.what: The port weights define an inner product on port functions, and the classification verdict is the nearest compact Lie family in that metric.
rows.why: These rules turn the carrier's bracket into a definite gauge-algebra classification even when it matches no compact type exactly.
rows.statement: The normalized port-dual measure is read as the diagonal carrier inner product on port functions, and the discriminator verdict is the nearest classified compact family in the induced bracket-space metric.

rows.name: compact-Lie classification inputs
rows.what: Three classical facts about compact Lie groups: the center-plus-semisimple splitting, the surjective exponential map, and the classification of simple compact Lie algebras.
rows.why: OPH's gauge classification uses them to identify the realized symmetry algebra from its structure and dimension.
rows.statement: Three classical facts enter the gauge classification: the splitting L = Z(L) + [L, L] of a compact Lie algebra, surjectivity of the exponential map on compact connected groups, and the classification of compact simple Lie algebras with its dimension list. The bridge steps declared as classical inputs in A5OPH.lean and TrichotomyCases.lean fall under this row.

rows.name: matter candidate grammar
rows.what: A matter candidate pairs a symmetry stratum of the twelve-port carrier with a small graded representation of its semisimple symmetry algebra.
rows.why: It fixes the search space and negative controls for matter content, so any selected matter multiplet is checked against a predeclared class.
rows.statement: A matter candidate is a pair (S, M): S a stratum of the classified compact locus of the fourteen-parameter equivariant Jacobi variety on the twelve-port carrier, and M a nonempty Z/2-graded complex module of the complexified semisimple bracket at S with zero abelian charges and total dimension at most twelve. The grammar, budget and decision rule are frozen in code/b15_matter_freeze/matter_class_freeze_v1.json.

rows.name: hadronic transport packet
rows.what: Measured electron-positron annihilation into hadrons supplies the hadronic vacuum polarization used to run the fine-structure constant.
rows.why: Running the electromagnetic coupling up to the Z-boson mass needs this hadronic contribution, which perturbation theory cannot compute.
rows.statement: The hadronic vacuum-polarization and spectral input is the pinned KNT19 e+e- hadronic payload (arXiv:1911.00367) registered in code/particles/hadron/empirical_ee_hadrons_sources.yaml. It is compare and transport data for the alpha(m_Z) anchor transport.

rows.name: clock and energy calibration anchors
rows.what: Internal clock counts and energy gaps carry no laboratory units; attaching them to measured clocks and energy standards in SI units is an empirical step.
rows.why: Every OPH statement in seconds, hertz or joules depends on this attachment, including physical temperatures, frequencies and Newton's constant.
rows.statement: Internal modular charge, energy gaps and repair-step counts carry no laboratory units. The attachment to measured clock and energy standards, including conversion to SI units, is an empirical calibration input.

rows.name: Lorentzian continuum limit of the finite event order
rows.what: The finite event order and its Lorentz carrier become a continuum spacetime through one faithful refinement family with a unique Lorentzian limit.
rows.why: Any reading of OPH's finite causal order as smooth spacetime, and every theorem using stable causality or global hyperbolicity, rests on it.
rows.statement: Promotion of the finite source event order and the one-plus-three Lorentz carrier to a physical continuum needs one source-selected refinement family with physical event and link identification, two-way order-cone-faithful placements, dense isotropic link directions, calibrated count-to-volume, independent dimension, manifoldlikeness and topology tests, a unique Lorentzian limit and convergent curvature estimators. Stable causality or global hyperbolicity is a further condition wherever a theorem invokes it.

rows.name: proposed fundamental numerical parameters P and N
rows.what: OPH proposes two fundamental free numbers: a screen-grain parameter P fixed by a self-consistency equation, and a capacity parameter N.
rows.why: Couplings and scales derived through OPH's closure maps depend on these two numbers.

rows.statement: A uniform cofinal cyclicity receipt holds for every half-line used, every nested pair consumed by Borchers-Wiesbrock is standard with a cyclic relative commutant, and weak additivity holds cofinally on the null blow-up net.

rows.name: Protected-defect register on the native process
rows.what: Protected defects carry a five-level code, three plus two levels, whose classes are conserved Z6 flux classes that observers read.
rows.why: It gives particle-like defects conserved colour, weak and hypercharge labels, the record through which OPH reads defects as charged particles.
rows.statement: The protected defects of the native process carry the declared five-level code C^3 + C^2 as a commuting record register whose classes are Z6 face fluxes of seam links, with the vector and spinor levels carrying port loads 2 and -3, so that each defect's flux class is a record that observers read and that the native dynamics conserves.

rows.name: Gauss-sector central action and antisymmetric occupation
rows.what: On gauge-invariant states a full 2 pi rotation acts as minus one raised to the number of quanta, and occupations are antisymmetric.
rows.why: It is the spin-statistics link: excitations with odd quanta behave as fermions and obey Pauli exclusion.
rows.statement: On a Gauss-invariant state the code, register and link-end factors of the central element z = -1 of the binary icosahedral group multiply to +1, so the 2pi rotation equals (-1)^(number of quanta) (P2); occupations of the five-level code are lifted antisymmetrically, and the filled reference that would force the antisymmetric lift is not computed (P4).

rows.why: Read on the five-level code these phases generate S(U(3) x U(2)), the Standard Model gauge group, so the gauge symmetry rests on them.
rows.statement: Independent continuous phases on the twelve ports extend the finite group of native transports; read on the five-level code they generate S(U(3) x U(2)). No law that writes these phases is derived.

rows.statement: A classical carrier mode is a quantum particle only with (Q1) a positive-energy quantization with physical Hilbert space, (Q2) a two-point function whose Kallen-Lehmann measure contains a positive-residue one-particle pole, and (Q3) the asymptotic-state or LSZ hypotheses of the phase, including a deconfined sector for a coloured carrier.

rows.what: The declared scalar oscillator and the three-axis quantum walk on the three-torus run natively on the model's carrier with a physical step duration.
rows.why: It lets the vacuum-fidelity and quantum-transport results proved for these declared processes count as statements about the model itself.
rows.statement: The declared positive finite scalar oscillator Hamiltonian with its original vacuum and symmetric kick/drift programs (code/m1_vacuum_fidelity) and the declared three-axis unitary Pauli walk on the three-torus with its quasienergy vacuum (code/m1_quantum_transport) are realized by the native process of the executable model on its own carrier, with a physical step duration.
